title: The Lefschetz Theorem on Hyperplane Sections
notes: Welcome the class to this lecture on the Lefschetz Theorem on Hyperplane Sections. We will begin by contextualizing how Morse theory, traditionally a tool of real differential topology, becomes a powerful method to study the homology and cohomology of complex algebraic varieties. The key idea is to slice a variety with a hyperplane and study the topological changes in the complement, which behaves beautifully due to complex dimensions.

title: Lecture Plan & Core Concepts
notes: Here is our course map and key checkpoints. We start with the classical Morse Lemma to understand local critical points, move to the global handle attachment theorem, and then show how the complex algebraic structure imposes dramatic constraints on the Morse index. Finally, we state the Lefschetz Hyperplane Section Theorem and look at its computational consequences on Betti numbers and Hodge structures.

title: The Morse Lemma: Local Coordinate Models
notes: The Morse Lemma is a local classification result. It states that near any nondegenerate critical point of a smooth function, we can choose coordinates such that the function is strictly quadratic. The number of negative signs in this coordinate representation is the index lambda of the critical point, representing the number of independent directions of downward curvature.

title: Global Morse Theory: Building Spaces via Handles
notes: In global Morse theory, as our height parameter crosses a critical value, the topology of the sublevel set changes by the attachment of a cell. This cell, or handle, has a dimension exactly equal to the Morse index lambda. This cellular decomposition means that homology in degrees strictly less than lambda remains stable and unchanged as we pass the critical level.

title: Complex Geometry Restricts the Morse Index
notes: This is the pivotal transition to algebraic geometry. When we examine a smooth affine complex variety of complex dimension n, its real dimension is two n. In the real setting, a Morse function could have critical points of index up to two n. However, due to the complex structure and the properties of the complex Hessian, the index of an algebraic distance function is strictly bounded by n.

title: The Lefschetz Theorem on Hyperplane Sections
notes: We now state the Lefschetz Hyperplane Section Theorem. Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension n, and Y a smooth hyperplane section. The theorem asserts that the cohomology of the pair vanishes below degree n. Consequently, the restriction map is an isomorphism in all degrees below n minus one, and remains injective at the middle dimension. This allows us to understand X using its lower-dimensional slice.

notes: Let us examine this visually. In this inline SVG diagram, we see the projective variety X sliced by a hyperplane H, cutting out the smooth intersection Y. Any topological cycle of low dimension on X can be continuously deformed or pushed down to lie entirely inside the hyperplane section Y. Only when we reach the middle dimension do we find cycles that cannot be retracted, as they are blocked by the topology of the affine complement.

title: Betti Numbers & The Hodge Ledger
notes: Here we inspect the numeric Betti numbers and the Hodge ledger of a toy algebraic surface of dimension two. The Betti numbers are one, zero, seven, zero, one. When we intersect this surface with a smooth curve Y, the Lefschetz theorem guarantees that the restriction is an isomorphism on H0 and is injective on H1, showing perfect alignment with our algebraic ledger calculations.

title: Summary & Pedagogical Pitfalls
notes: We conclude with the major takeaways and warning flags. Never forget that the hyperplane section must be smooth and transverse, which is guaranteed generically by Bertini's theorem. The Morse function is analyzed on the open affine complement, not the projective variety directly. By understanding these steps, we see how complex structures cleanly restrict topology.
